issues.explanation: For a life-threatening accident, 'Babies' as a salient auditory trigger is hard to connect clinically unless the accident specifically involved infants/crying, which is not supported by the rest of the profile. The other trigger items (intrusive thoughts, nightmare residue) are generic trauma reactivation cues, making this item stand out as trauma-incongruent.

issues.item: Maladaptive Strategies: Never Alone: make sure never to be alone with another person
issues.explanation: 'Make sure never to be alone with another person' suggests avoidance linked to fear of being accused of harming someone or of interpersonal/sexual threat, which is not coherently supported by the accident trauma type, threat items, or appraisals. The rest of the profile is organized around generalized danger/vulnerability, not being alone with another person specifically.

issues.item: Negative Appraisals: Humiliation: I feel permanently humiliated by what happened
issues.explanation: 'I feel permanently humiliated by what happened' is not impossible after an accident, but here it lacks support from the other selected items. The threat and strategy items focus on physical danger and hypervigilance, while no memory or trigger content suggests shame-based social exposure. In this profile, humiliation is the least coherent appraisal and appears disconnected from the accident-focused formulation.

vignette:
The accident happened on a Tuesday evening. Three years ago, Somsak was driving home from the outpatient clinic where he works as a physical therapist when a delivery truck ran a red light and T‑boned his sedan. He spent two weeks in the trauma unit with a fractured pelvis and internal bleeding, then months in rehabilitation. Physically he healed enough to return to work, but something in him never quite settled. He had come to believe that his body was now permanently damaged—a conviction that surfaced every time he felt a twinge in his lower back or had to brace himself against a heavy patient transfer. “You can never know who will harm you,” he would think, scanning the faces of drivers in the parking lot. The accident had taught him that safety was an illusion.

At the clinic, Somsak began to notice that certain sounds undid him. When a metal pan clattered onto the floor in the gym, his whole body jerked as if the collision were happening again. The startle response was immediate and humiliating; afterward he would feel his heart pound and his concentration dissolve, leaving him staring at the treatment table unable to remember the patient’s exercise plan. These loud noises—the crash of a dropped weight, the sudden bang of a door—triggered not only a racing pulse but also a fresh wave of the old belief: his body could not be trusted, and danger could arrive without warning. Waking from nightmares about the crash left him lying rigid in the dark, the residue of the dream pressing him into a certainty that he was still vulnerable, still at risk.

To manage this dread, Somsak developed a set of quiet rituals. At the start of every shift he cleaned and reorganized the treatment room, aligning bottles and wiping down surfaces until everything felt orderly. He told himself this gave him a measure of control—a way to push back against the chaos the accident had introduced. He also began mentally rehearsing worst‑case scenarios for each patient, imagining what could go wrong during a transfer or an exercise and how he would respond. And he started checking his environment constantly, scanning the clinic for anything that might serve as a weapon or a hazard: the scissors on the counter, the fire extinguisher, the heavy dumbbells. These strategies were driven by a deep, unshakable conviction that he was fragile and the world was hostile—the negative appraisals of his body and the malice of others. But the scanning, in particular, worked against him. The more he looked for threats, the more he found them: a patient’s crutch leaning at an odd angle, a cable on the pulley machine that might snap. He saw potential weapons everywhere, and this hypervigilance kept his startle response primed, so that even a colleague’s friendly tap on the shoulder made him flinch. Flinching, in turn, reinforced the sense that danger was imminent and that his own reactions were out of his control. The cycle fed itself: each startle brought back the intrusive image of the truck’s grille; each unwanted memory sharpened his fear of harm; each rehearsal reminded him that he could not rely on his own body to protect him.

Somsak’s wife noticed first that he had stopped laughing, then that he was avoiding the couple’s weekend hikes. He told her he was just tired. In truth, he was terrified of being out in the open, where the sound of a passing truck or even a gust of wind could send him back into the moment of impact. At work, his difficulty concentrating had begun to affect his notes; several times he had to recheck a patient’s range‑of‑motion measurements because his mind had gone blank during the test. He cleaned his treatment table three times a day now, and he rehearsed the clinic’s emergency evacuation route every morning. What finally brought him to the clinic door was the nightmare that woke him screaming his wife’s name—and the feeling, when he opened his eyes, that the threat had not passed at all. He hoped that talking about it might make the world feel safe again, but he was also afraid that nothing could.
